entry.title: Let a session outlive the process that issued it (#57)
entry.content:
Let a session outlive the process that issued it (#57)

Every deploy asked for the password again. Sessions were held in a Map in
process memory, so a restart forgot every one of them; the seven-day
lifetime never mattered because a deploy always came first.

The cookie now carries its own expiry and a signature over it, keyed off the
configured password, so a fresh process recognises a session it never
issued. The password is already in the environment and stable across
restarts, so this needs no new configuration and no storage.

Rotating GAFU_ACCESS_PASSWORD now invalidates every outstanding session. The
Map did not do that: it kept honouring sessions issued under the old
password until they expired.

What is given up: logout revokes for as long as the process lives, but a
restart forgets the revocation, so a signed-out cookie would be honoured
again until its expiry. Reaching that requires having captured the cookie
before sign-out, since sign-out clears it. For a single-owner deployment
behind a password, with a bounded lifetime, that is a smaller cost than a
login on every deploy -- but it is a real one, so it is stated here and in
the code rather than left to be discovered.

Tests cover the case the Map failed: a cookie issued by one instance is
accepted by a separately constructed one, refused after the password
changes, refused when its expiry is edited without re-signing, and refused
once that expiry passes.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Stop asking for a candidate on punctuation (#56)
entry.content:
Stop asking for a candidate on punctuation (#56)

"provider returned canonicalKey !? : where !?: was supplied": the model
answered `!? :` for a token whose canonicalKey is `!?:`, inserting a space,
and that one candidate rejected its batch.

Kuromoji files an unrecognised run of symbols under 名詞/サ変接続, so `!?`,
`...` and `...♪` arrive as nouns and earn vocabulary candidates. With no
reading, their canonicalKey is punctuation plus the empty-reading colon --
`!?:`, `...♪:` -- which is exactly the kind of string a model tidies.
Subtitles are full of them.

Precomputing the key in #54 was necessary but not sufficient: supplying a
string does not stop a model reformatting one that looks like a typo. The
answer is not to ask. A token now earns a candidate only if its surface
contains a letter or a number, so punctuation is absent from the payload
and from what the answer is compared against.

The predicate lives with the expectations, so the payload, the per-batch
check, and the run-level check move together, and the fake providers use it
too rather than their own copy of contentParts.

promptVersion goes to preparation-v4. Two batches completed under v3 and
hold candidates v4 does not expect, which would read as invented evidence
at run level; completed batches are not re-checked, so they have to be
asked again.

Real words are unaffected, including those with no reading: グリズリー, Wi,
and 24 still earn candidates and still carry the trailing colon.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Hold the API key only in the server environment (#55)
entry.content:
Hold the API key only in the server environment (#55)

The key was held in process memory and entered through settings, so every
restart discarded it. That is six re-entries across today's deploys, and it
made an environment-supplied key ambiguous: a key typed in settings won the
session and then silently reverted to the environment's on the next deploy,
while "Remove API key" cleared a copy that came back on restart.

The key is now a deployment value and nothing else. It is read from
OPENAI_API_KEY at startup, held in process memory, and verified against the
provider on first preflight. There is no route, form, or session copy that
could disagree with the environment.

Removed: PUT and DELETE /api/provider/key, replaceProviderKey and
removeProviderKey from the LearningMaterial seam, replace and remove from
ProviderKeyCustody, the settings form and its remove button, and the
revision counter that existed only to order concurrent replacements.
Settings now reports which provider and model are configured and whether
the environment supplied a key, and names OPENAI_API_KEY when it did not.

This keeps the phase-2 invariant that matters -- the key never reaches
SQLite, a backup, a response, or a log -- while dropping the browser entry
path that phase-2 also described. Railway stores it encrypted at rest and
can seal it so it is write-only, which is strictly better custody than a
value retyped into a form after every deploy.

phase-2.md is updated to match rather than left contradicting the code: the
custody bullet, the settings paragraph, the LearningMaterial type, and the
two adversarial cases that were about replacing and removing a key.

The Playwright harness supplies OPENAI_API_KEY, because the key can no
longer be entered through the page it is testing.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Check completeness per batch and supply the keys the model must not d…
entry.content:
Check completeness per batch and supply the keys the model must not derive (#54)

Audit of every field the validator compares against what the payload
supplies, prompted by three consecutive failures that were each a case of
the model being asked to reproduce something it had not been given.

Verified sound: token spans reconstruct exactly (0 mismatches over 54
tokens from the real analyzer), and `contentParts` matches the instruction
wording.

Three defects, all confirmed by measurement.

Completeness was checked only once a run was whole. The real analyzer plus
grammar detector oblige about 5,914 annotations for a 352-cue episode --
24 content tokens and 60 grammar annotations per 5 cues, so roughly 330 per
batch -- and `validateCompleteEvidence` demanded exact set equality over all
of them. It ran only at `complete`, after all 18 batches were paid for, and
`preparation.ts` then reset every batch in the run, discarding the lot. The
most expensive failure was also the most likely.

Cues partition into batches, so agreement on every batch is agreement on
the manifest. Completeness, duplication, and canonicalKey are now compared
as each batch commits: the same discrepancy is caught, but it costs one
batch to ask again rather than the whole run. The run-level check remains as
a final assertion and should no longer be reachable first. Both call the
same comparison, so they cannot drift, and the detail now names what was
omitted or altered instead of only a count.

canonicalKey had to be built from a rule the rule did not cover.
`canonicalVocabulary` is `lemma:reading` with a trailing colon when the
reading is null, which the instruction "canonicalKey is exactly
lemma:reading" does not describe: 6 of 26 content tokens on katakana and
latin text have no reading, and Shirokuma Cafe is full of them. It is now
precomputed into the payload for tokens and grammar occurrences alike, so
the model copies a string.

The content-token filter was the model's job. 30 of 54 tokens are
non-content and had to be skipped by judging broadPartOfSpeech the same way
the validator does; any disagreement changed the count. The payload now
carries only the tokens that earn a candidate, so its size fixes the
answer's size.

promptVersion is bumped to preparation-v3, and this one is required rather
than cosmetic: batches completed under v2 were never checked for
canonicalKey, because that comparison only happened once a run was whole.
Leaving them completed would let them bypass the per-batch check. This
starts a fresh run and does not reuse previously completed batches.

`contentParts` was copied in four files; preparation's copy now has one
home, shared by the payload, the per-batch check, and the run-level check.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Label cues shortly instead of asking the model to echo a digest (#53)
entry.content:
Label cues shortly instead of asking the model to echo a digest (#53)

Analysis failed with "invalidCueEvidence (unknown cue
cue-v1:sha256:178923d4604444437ac0c1636a15d8732431dc2)". The span problem
from #52 is gone; this is the other branch of the validator, and the same
class of defect one layer up.

A cue id is `cue-v1:sha256:` plus a 64-character digest, and the contract
asks the model to echo it on every candidate. A batch of 20 cues asks for a
candidate per content token, so that is roughly 120 ids -- about 7,700
characters of pure entropy to reproduce byte-perfect, and a single slip
rejects all 120. The id above is 39 hex characters where 64 were sent: it
dropped 25 characters mid-transcription.

Asking a model to copy an opaque digest is the same mistake as asking it to
count UTF-16 code units. Cues are now labelled `c1`, `c2`, ... in what the
adapter serializes, and the labels are translated back to cue ids as the
answer is decoded. The model echoes two characters instead of seventy-eight.

`retrieve` now takes the batch, because rebuilding the labels is the only
way to read a polled response back into cue ids.

A label the batch does not name is reported as `malformedStructure` naming
the label, rather than surfacing as an unknown cue id. It is a modelling
error about a two-character token, not evidence about a cue.

As in #52 this touches only what the adapter serializes and decodes, not
`AnalyzedCue`, so manifest digests and already-completed batches are
unaffected, and `promptVersion` is unchanged.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Give the model a grammar surface to copy instead of an offset to comp…
entry.content:
Give the model a grammar surface to copy instead of an offset to compute (#52)

Analysis failed with "invalidCueEvidence (invalid normalized span for
cue-v1:sha256:b92901dd...)". The model was not at fault, and neither was
the validator.

The candidate contract asks for `surface` plus a span whose slice
reconstructs it, and the instructions say to copy both from the supplied
cue. Tokens do supply `surface`, so vocabulary candidates copy it and
verify. Grammar evidence supplied only `canonicalForm` and `spans` -- no
surface anywhere -- and a canonical form is a label, not the text. Of 317
declared forms, 84 begin with the placeholder `〜`, and others are
metalinguistic: `受身形`, `命令形 (動詞)`, `の ( nominalizer )`,
`〜ない (る-Verb Negative)`. On one ordinary sentence, 18 of 25 detected
forms had a canonical form that does not occur in the cue at all.

So for grammar the model could only copy the label, which cannot verify, or
count UTF-16 code units into Japanese itself, which is unreliable. Either
way one bad span rejects its whole batch of roughly 120 candidates, which
is why this recurred on every run.

The adapter now flattens each grammar occurrence to the token shape and
includes the surface, sliced locally from the cue it already holds:

  { canonicalForm, surface, span }

Verification is unchanged and nothing is repaired after the fact; the model
is simply given the thing it was always asked to reproduce. This touches
only what the adapter serializes, not `AnalyzedCue`, so manifest digests
and already-completed batches are unaffected.

`instructions` and `promptVersion` are deliberately unchanged: the task
definition is the same, and "copy surface exactly from the supplied cue"
merely becomes satisfiable for grammar. Bumping the version would orphan
every completed batch and repay for them.

Also give zz-phase2-study a real time budget. It creates fourteen Grammar
Cards one at a time and waits for a generated review, measuring 28-29s
against Playwright's 30s default, so it failed whenever anything else
shared the machine. I twice attributed that to contention, which was the
symptom; the budget was the cause.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Ask again for a rejected response instead of replaying it (#51)
entry.content:
Ask again for a rejected response instead of replaying it (#51)

* Ask again for a rejected response instead of replaying it

Analysis failed with `invalidCueEvidence`: a response arrived, decoded
against the schema, and then failed local span verification. The batch was
left dispatched with its response id, so resuming retrieved the same
known-bad output from provider-side retention and re-failed on it
identically -- no new request at all -- until retention expired, at which
point it demanded a duplicate-charge decision:

  round 1: failed invalidCueEvidence [uncertain,...] submit()=1 retrieve()=0
  round 2: failed invalidCueEvidence [uncertain,...] submit()=0 retrieve()=1
  round 3: failed invalidCueEvidence [uncertain,...] submit()=0 retrieve()=1

preparation.ts already states the rule for the whole-run case: invalid
output is safe to charge but not safe to cache. Apply it per batch. A
response that arrived and was rejected locally -- invalid cue evidence,
malformed structure, incomplete output, or refusal -- now releases the
checkpoint to `pending`, whether it arrived from submit or from retrieve.
The batch still does not complete, as phase-0.md requires of an invalid
span; it is simply asked again rather than replayed.

  round 1: failed invalidCueEvidence [pending,...] submit()=1 retrieve()=0
  round 2: failed invalidCueEvidence [pending,...] submit()=1 retrieve()=0

The failure detail is now shown. It was already carried in the snapshot and
discarded by the UI, which left `invalidCueEvidence` unactionable: the kind
cannot say whether a cue was unknown or a span did not reconstruct, nor
which of a batch's candidates was at fault. It now reads
"invalidCueEvidence (invalid normalized span for episode-1:001)".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Give the progress poller an interval

window.setInterval was called with no delay, which defaults to 0 and is
clamped by browsers to about 4ms. While a batch was in flight the page
therefore issued the live-snapshot GET hundreds of times a second, each one
querying SQLite and projecting findings, against the same server that was
waiting on the provider.

This was invisible while batches died in 60 seconds. Now that a batch
legitimately runs for minutes, it runs for the length of the analysis.

A batch takes minutes, so two seconds of granularity is ample.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Release rejected batches and verify a seeded key before offering anal…
entry.content:
Release rejected batches and verify a seeded key before offering analysis (#50)

Prepare stalled again after #49, this time with "last error: authentication"
and the duplicate-charge banner showing. Two defects.

A rejection was treated as a possible duplicate charge. #49 raised the
warning whenever a dispatch failed with no recorded response id, which is
true of every pre-dispatch failure -- including a 401, where the provider
refused to run the request and billed nothing. The batch also stayed
`uncertain` with no id, so it re-entered the unresolvable branch and
blocked every later batch, and the second round reported no failure at
all. That is the same latch #49 fixed for timeouts, reached by a different
route:

  round 1: failure=authentication duplicateCharge=true  [uncertain,...]
  round 2: failure=null           duplicateCharge=true  [uncertain,...]

Authentication, permission and rate-limit failures now release the
checkpoint to `pending`: nothing was generated, so there is nothing to
retrieve and nothing to repay, and fixing the cause needs no
duplicate-charge decision. A lost or abandoned connection is still
ambiguous and still warns.

  round 1: failure=authentication duplicateCharge=false [pending,...]
  round 2: failure=authentication duplicateCharge=false [pending,...]

A round that names its failure now reports it instead of retrying twice
more and burying it in "three rounds finished no new batches".

An unverified key claimed to be ready. The key is held only in memory and
seeded from OPENAI_API_KEY, so any restart -- including every deploy --
discards a key entered through settings and falls back to the environment.
A key that arrives that way never passes through `replace`, so it was
never verified, and `isConfigured` reported it ready. The scope panel then
offered to analyze with a key the provider rejects, 18 times.

Custody now verifies a seeded key once, on first preflight, and remembers
the answer. Only the provider's own refusal condemns a key; a verification
that cannot reach the provider leaves it usable, so a network blip does not
present as a bad key. `providerConfigured` is async to allow this.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Dispatch preparation batches in the background so a timeout is recove…
entry.content:
Dispatch preparation batches in the background so a timeout is recoverable (#49)

Analysis stalled at 0 of 18 batches with "three rounds finished no new
batches (last error: timeout)", and the duplicate-charge banner showing.

The run was not retrying: after the first round it stopped calling the
provider at all. A batch is marked `uncertain` before dispatch so a crash
cannot silently repay it. Recovering that state needs the provider's
response id, but a synchronous `store: false` call only yields the id
together with the output, so an interrupted call left nothing to look up
and `retrieve` returned no recovery. `uncertain` was therefore terminal:
every later round returned `paused` with `possibleDuplicateCharge` without
a request, so batch 1 blocked batches 2-18 permanently.

The wait was cut short because `timeoutMs` was 60s. That number was never
measured -- docs/evidence/phase-0-batching.md records that the paid smoke
gate never ran -- and it was sized against that script's 3-cue batches
while the server analyses 20 cues per batch, which runs to minutes.

phase-0.md allows recovery through provider idempotency or result
retrieval. Retrieval is available after all: background mode returns the
response id immediately and works with `store: false`, with provider-side
retention only long enough to poll, which the analysis disclosure already
covers. (`Idempotency-Key` is documented for the Ads and Agentic Commerce
APIs, not for /v1/responses, so it is not relied on.)

- Dispatch with `background: true`, commit the returned id via a new
  `markDispatched` before waiting, then poll GET /v1/responses/{id}.
  `timeoutMs` now bounds one HTTP call; `completionTimeoutMs` bounds the
  batch. A 404 while polling means the dispatch aged out and is reported
  as no recovery rather than as a transport failure.
- Carry `providerResponseId` on the `uncertain` checkpoint (schema v2).
  `possibleDuplicateCharge` now covers only the narrow window in which a
  dispatch was sent but its id was never committed.
- Send one batch per HTTP request. At minutes per batch a five-batch chunk
  held one request open long enough for an intermediary to drop it.
- Default the paid smoke script to the server's batch size, so the
  duration it reports bounds production batches.

Against a provider that times out on every wait, the run now completes a
batch per round instead of returning the same paused snapshot, and no
batch is paid for twice.

`completionTimeoutMs` remains an unmeasured upper bound; `bun run
spike:provider` is the gate that would calibrate it.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
